snippet_locator.section: Inosine: a purine metabolite at the metabolic-immune interface

snippets.text:
Inosine is a critical intermediary in the purine nucleotide metabolic pathway and is synthesized by gut microbiota such as Bifidobacterium pseudolongum, Lactobacillus johnsonii, and bacteria of the genus Olsenella (24). This microbial-derived metabolite plays essential roles in posttranscriptional gene regulation, modulation of metabolic enzyme activities, and integration into cellular signaling networks (25). Notably, immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy impairs gut barrier integrity, facilitating the translocation of inosine into the systemic circulation and subsequent activation of antitumor T cells, establishing inosine as the key molecule mediating the enhancement of ICB efficacy by these bacteria (24). 

Currently, inosine exerts three principal effects in antitumor therapy. Firstly, it markedly enhances tumor immunogenicity. Zhang et al. employed advanced metabolomic profiling to analyze plasma samples from melanoma-bearing mice undergoing ICI treatment, revealing a novel mechanism: inosine specifically inhibits ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 6 (UBA6) activity within tumor cells, leading to a marked increase in tumor immunogenicity (52). This dual-purpose finding identifies UBA6 as a therapeutic target and rationalizes inosine-based combination therapy. 

Secondly, inosine plays distinct roles in immune cell modulation and metabolic support. Microbial-derived inosine binds to adenosine A2A receptors on T lymphocytes, triggering activation of the cAMP-CREB signaling cascade. This pathway facilitates the differentiation and tumor infiltration of T helper 1 (Th1) cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME), amplifying antitumor immune responses (24). Thirdly, and most critically, inosine functions as a compensatory metabolic substrate that sustains T cell bioenergetics under glucose-restricted TME conditions. Wang et al. experimentally demonstrated that effector T cells utilize inosine as an alternative energy source during glucose deprivation, sustaining their survival, proliferation, and cytotoxic functions (53). Clinically, this dual functionality holds therapeutic promise.

title: Targeting the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: mechanistic interplay, therapeutic strategies, and translational applications-a narrative review
